newsitem.title: UK: Oil firm as traders shrug off imminent Iraq sales.
newsitem.headline: Oil firm as traders shrug off imminent Iraq sales.

text.p: Oil prices held gains on Tuesday as traders calculated that world markets would be able to digest an initial resumption of Iraqi oil exports without too much difficulty.
London North Sea Brent blend for September delivery was trading nine cents higher at the close at $19.54 a barrel.

Brent jumped 50 cents on Monday, taking prices to a 10-week high, after Iraq received United Nations approval for an aid distribution plan which paved the way for a second phase of exports under the UN's oil-for-food exchange.
Oil traders are expecting Iraqi crude held in storage at the Turkish pipeline outlet of Ceyhan and at Iraq's Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr to be available within a week.
They said buying interest for Iraqi crude in Baghdad's premier European market was reasonably strong.
"Several people will take on larger contracts than last time," said one potential buyer.
Iraq was expected to submit its pricing formula for the second round of oil exports to the U.N. sanctions committee for approval on Tuesday.
Under the terms of the oil accord, Iraq is allowed to sell $2.14 billion of oil over 180 days in two equal instalments. The deadline for its first billion dollars of sales is September 5.
Key to oil markets in the short term will be Iraqi export capacity. Analysts estimate Iraq is capable of moving some 1.3-1.4 million bpd but Baghdad says capacity stands at 2.5 million bpd.
At current prices Iraq would have to sell approaching two million bpd to reach its early September target.

Oil prices on Tuesday found continued support from the closure of some 175,000 barrels per day of Colombian crude supplies after the country's main pipeline was blown up twice and partially destroyed by a landslide at the weekend.
Engineers were repairing the crippled Cano Limon-Covenas pipeline but it will be at least Friday before it returns to full operations.

"Repair teams went in late Monday night to one section but haven't been authorised by the military to start work on the second dynamited section," a spokesman for the state-run oil company Ecopetrol said.
